sections.section_title: Clinical Approach to Progressive Proximal Weakness After GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Exposure
sections.description: Uses the case to frame the first steps when a patient presents with subacute proximal weakness, dysphagia, and dysphonia after new medication exposure (semaglutide), emphasizing early recognition of immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) versus toxic rhabdomyolysis.
key_points: Identify red flags: rapidly progressive proximal weakness, bulbar symptoms (dysphagia/dysphonia), CK markedly elevated, and functional decline.
Clarify medication and toxin history (statins, supplements like red yeast rice or certain mushrooms), recent infections, and exertional triggers.
Differentiate early: drug-induced rhabdomyolysis (acute CK spike with rapid dechallenge improvement) versus IMNM (progressive weakness despite drug withdrawal, need for immunosuppression).
Initial labs: CK, aldolase, AST/ALT, renal function, electrolytes, ESR/CRP, TSH; cardiac biomarkers if cardiopulmonary symptoms.
Physical exam: pattern of weakness (proximal > distal), bulbar/respiratory involvement, absence of dermatomyositis rash; screen for connective tissue disease signs.
Safety and disposition: evaluate swallowing/aspiration risk, respiratory status, hydration/renal support if needed; hold suspected offending agent.
Case anchor: CK rose from 337 U/L to 3992 U/L over 4 months after a single semaglutide dose, with progressive proximal weakness and bulbar symptoms.

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology and Immunology of Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy
sections.description: Details the immunopathology of IMNM, serologic subtypes, histopathologic hallmarks, and how drug exposures may trigger disease. Contrasts IMNM with toxic rhabdomyolysis and other inflammatory myopathies.
key_points: IMNM hallmarks: myofiber necrosis and regeneration with macrophage-rich myophagocytosis, complement (membrane attack complex) deposition, and relative paucity of lymphocytes.
Autoantibody-defined subsets: anti-HMGCR (statin-associated and non-statin), anti-SRP; approximately one-third are seronegative.
Clinical phenotype: aggressive proximal weakness, frequent dysphagia; possible respiratory and cardiac involvement (myocarditis, arrhythmias).
Immunologic mechanisms: humoral and complement-mediated injury; macrophage activation; potential autoantigen upregulation (e.g., HMGCR) in some contexts.
Triggers: statins are classic; other drugs and infections suspected; seronegative disease suggests additional, as yet unidentified antigens.
GLP-1 receptor agonists: not established triggers; hypothesized mechanisms include immune activation or metabolic stress unmasking muscle antigens; this case suggests a possible association.
Contrast with rhabdomyolysis: toxic or ischemic myocyte injury causing acute, high CK with rapid resolution after withdrawal and hydration; typically no need for immunosuppression.

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis of Subacute Proximal Weakness and CK Elevation
sections.description: Provides a structured differential and discriminators relevant to this case, including inflammatory, toxic, endocrine, neuromuscular junction, and critical illness etiologies.
key_points: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy: progressive weakness, bulbar involvement, MRI muscle edema, biopsy with necrosis/macrophages, often requires immunosuppression.
Toxic/drug-induced rhabdomyolysis: acute myalgias, pigmenturia, very high CK with rapid downtrend after drug cessation; biopsy shows necrosis without immune features.
Polymyositis/dermatomyositis/antisynthetase: dermal signs, interstitial lung disease, specific autoantibodies; biopsy shows endomysial/perifascicular features distinct from IMNM.
Inclusion body myositis: age >50, finger flexor/quadriceps weakness, poor steroid response; biopsy with rimmed vacuoles.
Endocrine/metabolic myopathies: hypo/hyperthyroidism, Cushing's, electrolyte disorders; CK often modest, improves with endocrine correction.
Critical illness myopathy/neuropathy: ICU exposure, sepsis, steroids/neuromuscular blockers; EMG/NCS aid differentiation.
Neuromuscular junction disorders (e.g., myasthenia): fatigable weakness, ocular/bulbar predominance, normal CK.
Cardiac considerations: myocarditis vs stress cardiomyopathy; evaluate troponin, ECG, echocardiogram, cardiac MRI.
Hepatic transaminases: discern hepatic versus muscle sources; persistent steatohepatitis here explained background AST/ALT elevations.

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Workup and Causality Assessment in Suspected Drug-Associated IMNM
sections.description: Outlines a stepwise evaluation including laboratory tests, imaging, electrodiagnostics, muscle biopsy interpretation, assessment of extramuscular involvement, and structured causality analysis for suspected medication triggers.
key_points: Serologies: myositis panel (anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP, antisynthetase, Mi-2, MDA5, TIF1-γ, NXP2); recognize that up to one-third of IMNM is seronegative.
Muscle enzymes and inflammatory markers: CK, aldolase, AST/ALT, ESR/CRP; track CK/strength longitudinally.
Muscle MRI: symmetric edema in affected muscle groups supports active myositis; guides biopsy site selection.
EMG (if available): irritable myopathy pattern; supportive but not specific.
Muscle biopsy: necrotic/regenerating fibers, macrophage infiltration (CD68), acid phosphatase activity, membrane attack complex on fibers; scant lymphocytes (rare CD3) and perivascular cells.
Extramuscular evaluation: swallow study, pulmonary function (including MIP/MEP), echocardiogram and cardiac MRI if cardiac symptoms/biomarker elevation.
Interpretation of liver tests: consider muscle contribution when CK is high; correlate with imaging/biopsy for NAFLD/NASH.
Causality assessment: apply WHO-Uppsala Monitoring Centre criteria—temporal relationship, dechallenge response, alternative causes excluded; rechallenge generally unethical in severe reactions.

Case anchor: negative myositis-specific antibodies, MRI edema, biopsy consistent with IMNM, and clinical improvement after corticosteroids/IVIG and semaglutide avoidance support probable drug association.

sections.section_title: Management of IMNM: Immunotherapy, Supportive Care, and Comorbidity Considerations
sections.description: Summarizes evidence-based treatment strategies for IMNM, indications for combination therapy, monitoring, prevention of complications, and alternatives for metabolic disease management when GLP-1 receptor agonists are avoided.
key_points: Initial therapy: high-dose glucocorticoids (e.g., IV methylprednisolone pulses followed by oral prednisone ~1 mg/kg/day).
Early adjuncts: IVIG (2 g/kg over 2–5 days) for severe weakness, bulbar or respiratory involvement, or inadequate steroid response.
Steroid-sparing agents (if needed): methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate; rituximab for refractory disease; tailor to serology, severity, and comorbidities.
Monitoring: serial CK and strength testing; assess swallowing and respiratory function; cardiac monitoring if initial involvement suspected.
Steroid taper: guided by clinical and CK response; aim to minimize exposure to reduce infection, metabolic, and bone risks.
Infection prevention: vaccination review, consideration of PJP prophylaxis with prolonged high-dose steroids or multi-agent immunosuppression; early recognition of sepsis.
Rehabilitation and nutrition: PT/OT to counter deconditioning; swallow therapy and nutritional support to prevent aspiration and malnutrition.

Medication counseling: avoid re-exposure to the suspected trigger (here, GLP-1 receptor agonists); consider alternatives for obesity/diabetes (lifestyle therapy, SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin if appropriate, bariatric referral).
Comorbidity management: address NAFLD/NASH, cardiovascular risk; cautious lipid management avoiding statins in active or prior HMGCR-positive IMNM.
Case anchor: marked CK and functional improvement with short-course steroids and a single IVIG cycle; successful steroid taper over 2 months; no further immunotherapy required.

sections.description: Provides expectations for outcomes, recommended follow-up, patient counseling, and high-yield takeaways to avoid common pitfalls.
key_points: Prognosis: many patients improve with prompt immunotherapy; seronegative IMNM can still achieve remission, though some require prolonged therapy.
Follow-up: frequent early visits (every 2–4 weeks) to adjust steroids and monitor CK/strength; extend intervals once stable; reassess swallowing and cardiac status as indicated.
Relapse prevention: gradual steroid taper, introduce steroid-sparing agents if relapse occurs or taper is constrained by side effects.
Avoid class re-exposure: counsel against rechallenge with GLP-1 receptor agonists after suspected IMNM; document adverse reaction prominently.
Pharmacovigilance: report suspected cases to regulatory databases to refine understanding of rare adverse events.
Pearls: IMNM may be seronegative; biopsy is decisive. A rising CK and progressive weakness after drug withdrawal favors IMNM over rhabdomyolysis.
Pitfalls: attributing transaminitis solely to liver disease without considering muscle; missing bulbar or cardiac involvement; delaying immunotherapy while awaiting all test results.
Case outcome: full return to baseline off immunosuppression for months; normalization of cardiac imaging; sustained normal CK with continued avoidance of GLP-1 receptor agonists.
